Thomas R. Dew, Review of the Debate in the Virginia Legislature of 1831 and 1832, 1832
Theodore Gentilz, Fall of the Alamo, 1844

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources or paraphrases of them (see each document's sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which slavery shaped the development of Southern society in the period 1800–1848.

documents.title: Cotton takes off
documents.source: United States cotton crop figures, U.S. Department of Agriculture Circular 32 (National Bureau of Economic Research series A01028); cotton gin invented by Eli Whitney, 1793.
documents.sourcing: Government crop figures, collected long after the fact, showing the scale of the cotton boom.
documents.text: The United States cotton crop grew from 3,000 bales in 1790 to 73,000 bales in 1800. Whitney's cotton gin, invented in 1793, made short-staple cotton profitable to clean, and planters spread cotton farming across the South.

documents.title: The trade ends, slavery grows
documents.source: Act Prohibiting Importation of Slaves, 1807 (effective January 1, 1808); United States census counts.
documents.sourcing: A federal law and census counts; the law ended imports, not slavery itself.
documents.text: In 1808 Congress banned the importation of enslaved people into the United States, as the Constitution had allowed it to do. Yet the enslaved population kept growing, from 893,602 in 1800 to 1,538,022 in 1820, by natural increase and the domestic slave trade.

documents.title: A conspiracy in Charleston
documents.source: Paraphrase of the record of the Denmark Vesey conspiracy, Charleston, South Carolina, 1822.
documents.sourcing: A course-book account based on trial records, which white officials wrote and may have shaped.
documents.text: In 1822, Denmark Vesey, a free Black carpenter in Charleston, South Carolina, was accused of planning a rising of enslaved people. Vesey and dozens of others were hanged, and South Carolina tightened its laws on Black movement and assembly.

documents.title: Turner's rebellion
documents.source: Paraphrase of the record of Nat Turner's rebellion, Southampton County, Virginia, August 1831.
documents.sourcing: A summary of the rebellion and its aftermath, drawn from Virginia records.
documents.text: In August 1831, Nat Turner led enslaved people in Southampton County, Virginia, in a rebellion that killed more than fifty white people. The rising was put down, Turner was hanged, and the Virginia legislature debated emancipation in the winter of 1831–32 before rejecting it and tightening the state's slave codes.

documents.title: A professor defends slavery
documents.source: Thomas R. Dew, Review of the Debate in the Virginia Legislature of 1831 and 1832 (1832). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A slaveholding professor writing to defend slavery after the Virginia debate failed.
documents.text: “In the debate in the Virginia legislature, no speaker insinuated even, we believe that the slaves in Virginia were not treated kindly; and all too agreed that they were most abundantly fed, and we have no doubt but that they form the happiest portion of our society.”

documents.title: A positive good
documents.source: John C. Calhoun, Senate speech, February 6, 1837. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A Southern senator answering abolitionist petitions in the Senate.
documents.text: “I hold that in the present state of civilization, where two races of different origin, and distinguished by color, and other physical differences, as well as intellectual, are brought together, the relation now existing in the slaveholding States between the two, is, instead of an evil, a good—a positive good.”

documents.title: Texas joins the Union
documents.source: Paraphrase of the record of Texas annexation, 1845; see Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.13 C.
documents.sourcing: A summary of annexation; the nine-year delay itself shows how slavery shaped national politics.
documents.text: In 1845 the United States annexed Texas, a republic founded by American settlers who had brought slavery with them onto cotton land. Texas entered as a slave state, and its admission had been delayed for nine years because presidents feared it would deepen the sectional fight over slavery.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which slavery shaped the development of Southern society, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of slavery's shaping does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the market revolution, the growth of cotton, or the rise of abolitionism.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing the content of at least three documents relevant to the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or using six without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific relevant example not in the documents, such as the Missouri Compromise, Tocqueville's Ohio-Kentucky comparison, or the domestic slave trade.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to outside knowledge with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the audience, purpose, historical situation, or point of view of at least two documents shapes the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document's author without explaining how it shapes the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for a complex argument, such as qualifying the thesis by showing where slavery shaped Southern society and where Southerners resisted or reshaped it, or who gained and who paid the price.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Slavery shaped the development of Southern society to a great extent between 1800 and 1848, remaking its economy, its politics, and its identity, yet enslaved people and white fear also shaped that development in ways slaveholders did not choose.
Context: The market revolution and the cotton gin tied the South to British textile mills, while abolitionism attacked slavery from the North.
Evidence for shaping: the cotton crop boomed after the gin (Doc 1); the enslaved population grew even after imports ended (Doc 2); Dew and Calhoun defended slavery as good (Docs 5, 6); Texas carried slavery west and delayed annexation (Doc 7).
Evidence for limits and fear: Vesey's conspiracy and Turner's rebellion were answered with hangings and tighter laws (Docs 3, 4), showing a society shaped by fear of the people it held enslaved.
Complexity: Slavery built Southern wealth and pride, and it also built the fear that governed Southern law; the same system that enriched planters made white Southerners police their own society.
